analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 41 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsoring, the bill was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently repeal the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, the two taxes levied when very large fortunes pass to heirs. It keeps the gift tax in place but lowers its top rate to 35% and sets a $10 million lifetime gift exemption. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. The estate tax applies only to the portion of an estate above roughly $13 million per person (about $26 million per married couple), so only a few thousand estates a year pay any of it; repeal would erase that tax bill entirely.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently repeals the estate tax for all deaths after enactment, ending the 18%–40% tax on very large estates.
Repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth passes directly to grandchildren or great-grandchildren, bypassing a taxed generation.
Keeps the gift tax but cuts its top rate from 40% to 35% and resets the lifetime gift exemption to $10 million, making it cheaper to move wealth out of an estate during life.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The revenue the estate tax raises from the largest estates would disappear, adding to deficits or requiring higher taxes, lower spending, or more borrowing to cover.

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates all federal revenue from the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes on the largest estates, increasing deficits unless the money is made up elsewhere.

The bill also cuts the gift tax's top rate to 35% and allows $10 million of tax-free lifetime gifting, letting wealthy families move assets out of reach of any future estate tax at a further revenue cost.

The estate tax already exempts the vast majority of estates — only the slice of an estate above roughly $13 million per person is taxed — so repeal's benefits would flow almost entirely to a few thousand of the wealthiest households each year rather than to typical family farms or businesses, which are the bill's stated focus.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: families above the roughly $13 million/$26 million exemption keep the entire tax on their excess wealth, which in the largest cases is many millions of dollars. The cost is broad: tens of billions in lost federal revenue over a decade, borne by everyone through deficits or other taxes. Because the tax already exempts nearly all estates and provides exemptions that shield most farms and small businesses, repeal is poorly targeted at the problem its sponsors describe.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never voted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, joined on the day of introduction by 41 other Senate Republicans, including Senator McConnell.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation; it was never reported out of committee.
The Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee held a hearing on January 24, 2024 (S.Hrg. 118-382), but the bill received no committee vote and no Senate floor action.
No Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill, and it never came to a vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax remained in place and the federal revenue it raises from the largest estates was preserved. Heirs of the very largest fortunes did not get the repeal they sought, and ordinary taxpayers were spared the revenue loss.

for.name: John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act of 2023 and recruited 41 Republican cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 41 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of most of the Senate Republican conference but far short of a majority of the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 30, 2023 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 Senate supporters were Republicans — 41 of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and no Democrat did — while the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates (estates above ~$13 million per person)
industries.note: Repeal would erase the only federal tax that applies specifically to multimillion- and billion-dollar inheritances, letting a few thousand very wealthy families a year pass on estates untaxed. The cost shows up not on their tax bills but in the federal budget everyone else shares.

Repeal would shrink the demand for elaborate estate-tax avoidance planning that the current tax generates. That is a loss for the industry, though it brings the public little direct benefit either way.
